Jasper Phillips wrote:
"I'm curious what cards you think are busted? Off the top of my head I feel
that Thought's Betrayed, Tomb of Ramses III, and Return to Innocence are,
although I vaguely remember others."

Those are the top three around here, and Mind Rape is added to the list as
well. Among our local play group, we play with RTI and Mind Rape banned, and
Tomb and TB turned into cards that still are sort of the same, but much less
busted (our local ToRIII requires the use of transfers to gain blood, and TB
just prevents strikes for a round). The other card that offends most of our
sensibillities is Banishment, and we play that it can only be called on a
younger vampire (so you cant build a weenie vote push deck that Banishes your
Justicar with a Caitif...), and suffice to say, we don't use Clan Hosers
either.

Another pretty wrong card is Dreams of the Sphinx, as it falls into the realm
of "cards that are really good, and every deck can benefit from, but you don't
have any, cause they are rare", but it really isn't that game affecting, so we
don't worry about it. For all intents and purposes, it is just like Short Term
Investment, but exactly a _billion_ times better. Sure, it is unique, but as
it only lasts 3 uses, you can pack multiples in your deck, and it seems highly
unlikely that anyone will ever contest it with you, as they will just wait till
yours is gone and then play theirs (just like the Tomb).

My preferred fix for TB is: "...Not usable against older vampires." It
allows the card to remain extremely powerful (as it should, IMO,
considering its reputation and blood cost), but adds a "catch" that makes
it dangerous to rely on completely.

One of the things that bothers me about TB is that it is more dangerous
against big vampires than small. If I design a combat deck around Wynn of
Lucretia, using plenty of combat cards with their particular disciplines,
I face the danger that I will be completely hosed and burnt by someone
with superior dominate who makes all their combat cards unusable. However
if I have a weenie combat deck, we can overwhelm a TB deck by sheer
multitud. Using 2 blood to hose weenies is not necessarily going to be
cost effective.

This seems to me to be the reverse of what the true situation should be.
It should be easier to dominate one's inferiors than one's superiors, who
have presumably stronger minds.

Lupus Australius wrote:
"My preferred fix for TB is: "...Not usable against older vampires." It allows
the card to remain extremely powerful (as it should, IMO, considering its
reputation and blood cost), but adds a "catch" that makes it dangerous to rely
on completely."

That is a good house rule, and fairly balancing. Our group finds the card
completely offensive in every aspect of its existance, so we neutered it to a
far greater extent, but yours is a good fix if you don't mind the concept of
the card as much as we do.

"One of the things that bothers me about TB is that it is more dangerous
against big vampires than small."

While this is a completely valid point about TB, it is also the sad truth about
the game in general: Large vampires are, in most cases, more a hinderance than
a benefit. Weenie decks are almost always more effective than decks based on
big guys, which I always found to be a distasteful aspect of the game. Why
should a deck built around Caitif and 2 point vampires be more effective than a
deck build around Justicars? In theory, it shouldn't be, but in general, such
decks usually are.

Sadly, the two cards that made large vampires into a stronger deck component,
Return to Innocence and Tomb of Ramses III, are pretty much universally
regarded as two of the most busted cards in the game.

Sure you can do these things, but frankly the game is more fun if
the whole thing doesn't revolve around Tomb of Ramses, Thoughts
Betrayed, Mind Rape, and the Return to Innocence. I like a little
more to my "meta game" than seeing who can play the most power cards.

Oh, and do you really think Direct Intervention is going to save your ass?
Right, _if_ your opponent doesn't have sudden reversal, or another TB.
What are the odds of that? A tight deck is going to laugh at your once per
time round the table, pool losing cancel. Might work if your opponent
has limited access to rare cards, but card rarity is _never_ a good
game balancer.

Furthermore, once you've stacked your deck with these rather narrow
defenses (even if they did work!), what do you do when your opponent
doesn't play those cards? Weep.

Also your arguments about the Tomb apply equally as well by analogy
to the Freak Drive decks that were the vogue before repeat actions
were banned, or weenie vote push back in the day. Just because something
can be stopped _does not_ mean it isn't broken. I remember hearing
that back when magic was the only game: "Oh, untapping your time
vault with enchantments isn't broken, since you could always disenchant
it, or just counterspell it when it comes out!". Wrong.

Anyway, You are entitled to your opinion, and can play how you want.
Personally I would like it if the rules team would figure out play balance
because tournament play would be interesting, but not in a broken game.

Whoa! You don't consider RtI and the Tomb busted? First, RtI... It costs 4
blood. This is it's only limiting factor. So, you can't use it if your vamp
has burned too much blood. But the fact that your vampire is burned is not a
problem, since it's a sure ousting. No single card should allow you to oust
an opponent from a secure position. Especially when the card has no risk.
Hell... if you somehow get blocked (not enough Day Ops...), your vamp isn't
burned, and doesn't even spend the blood. It would be better if the vampire
were burned whether or not the action was successful, but still broken.

As for the Tomb, compare it to Art Museum and Eco Terrorists. AM and ET each
require a clan, and give you up to 1 pool a turn (to a specific type of
vampire), at a cost of 2 pool. It takes 2 turns for you to break even
(although 1 extra transfer may arguably be worth the extra pool). The Tomb
costs 3 pool and can give you 4 pool on the turn it comes out. It doesn't
require any clan and doesn't have any restrictions to which vampires you can
put blood on. Someone said that with the Tomb, you don't contest, because
it'll be going away soon. Why would it ever go away? Say you draw a 4
capacity and a 10 capacity in your starting crypt. You bring out the 4 cap,
and then leave the 10 capacity in your uncontrolled region for the rest of
the game. Any time he starts to get too much blood, transfer it off. If you
can get an Information Highway, there is a preposterous potential for blood
gain. The Tomb is just far too strong. There are a good number of ways to
fix it, but the tournament solution is to ignore it and let anyone who
doesn't have a Tomb lose.

> And I don't agree about TB being bad either - it's
> certainly no worse in principle than IG, HL or FR.

Well... TB isn't as bad as most broken cards, but it's still much nastier
than IG, HL, or FR. Immortal Grapple is very strong, and in fact is probably
the only thing that keeps Potence as a viable discipline. But it is really
only an offensive card. You can stop Thaumaturgists and Assamites, but
mainly IG just makes them stop running away so you can hit them. Plus, it
requires close range, which Potence can't assure on its own. HL and FR both
have a huge added stipulation. If you never block or get blocked, you can't
use them, and your vampire still has to survive the first combat. Thoughts
Betrayed is offensive *and* defensive, has no requirements. The only thing
that makes it almost balanced is the blood cost. It's a bit pricey to hit
Anarchs with it. If it were only usable against younger vampires, and/or
cost 3 blood instead of 2, it would be okay.

race to see who gets one first. Banning them is a much easier solution.
Fixing them is viable, but it's difficult to agree on house rules, and when

Dallas Card wrote:
"I'm amazed no one has mentioned Kiss of Ra. In my opinion, this is far worse

Ah well, I guess fortitude just wasn't powerful enough before, eh?"

Yah, I agree that Kiss of Ra is pretty wack, but around here, blocking isn't
all that important, so it being risky to block a vampire with superior
Fortitude is a price we are willing to pay (that, and no one around here has
any Kiss of Ra, but me, and I never think they are worth it to use them). The
only decks that ever try to block anything are base line intercept decks, and
there aren't that many of them.

Playing very focused decks reduces the need to intercept as a matter of course.
Rush decks are always tapped out cause they kill a vampire with every minion
with every action, and they don't have Wakes, as they muck up combat.
Bleed/Vote decks tend to have Deflection/Telepepathic Misdirection/Counter to
stop bleeds and they generally don't need to block votes due to anti-vote
reaction or speed. The only decks that ever consistently block are dedicated
intercept decks, like the local Tzimisczzeesk intercept deck. If a non
intercept deck discovers the hard way that his predator is packing Kiss of Ra,
he will just stop blocking vampires with superior Fortitude.

The issue of Kiss of Ra is very similar to the issues brought up by a recent
Dawn Opps/Drawing out the Beast thread--yes, it is potent, but blocking, unless
you are a dedicated intercept deck, is generally not important enough to worry
about Kiss of Ra that much, and no one can force you to block them. If it is
more important to keep your vampire alive than intercept a potential Kiss of Ra
user, don't intercept them.

Kiss of Ra hoses a dedicated intercept deck pretty hard (much like Deflection
hoses a S+B deck, or Majesty hoses a non Immortal Grapple combat deck), but
other than that, it doesn't have much effect on the game as a whole.

I have a couple, and I keep making all Fortitude stealthless bleed decks, and I
never manage to convince myself that Kiss of Ra is necessary. I prefer Dawn
Opps, so I can cycle my hand (and possibly burn someone...), and it doesn't
cost 2 blood to use.

All in all, again, Kiss of Ra doesn't strike me as that game affecting, as it
only really hoses dedicated Intercept decks, and only if they chose to
volunteer for the Kiss of Ra abuse. I suppose if you live in an enviornment
where all decks pack light intercept and wakes and try to block stuff all the
time, it would suck more, but that is not the situation around here.

I don't see RTI broken at all. First lets look at the efectiveness of the card
compared with Govern the Unaligned:
RTI costs 4 and a vampire bleed at +x
GTU cost 1 bleed at +2

Let us use a geneeric mid sized vampire, let's say Ozmo.

Over a sequence of turns Ozmo will bleed using RTI or GTU I am usuming that he
gets through each time, just for a point.

On any turn Ozmo has the following choice :
Ozmo uses RTI bleeds for 8
Ozmo uses GTU bleeds for 4

leaves us with the following:

Turn:1 2 3 4
RTI=8
GTU+RTI=12
GTU+GTU+RTI=16
GTU+GTU+GTU+RTI=20

This goes on.

take. Ozmo is more useful continually bleeding, then blowing his load in one

While your extensive analysis is a fairly accurate representation of the
situation you describe, it is not a really valid description of RTI. RTI is
not used on Ozmo to bleed you for 6. RTI is played on Inner Circle Members
(that got out for free with the Tomb or were Mind Raped away from an
opponent...) who come to bleed you unblockably for 15 and oust you in one
action.

RTI is a card that any vampire can use (a big one, preferably), you can't see
it coming (as no Discipline is required), and if it is coming for you and you
don't have a Deflection (or AI), you are ousted. One action, very little in
the way of defense. You are just gone. The inclusion of RTI in the set makes
it necessary to be playing Bleed Bounce in _every_ deck, or you will just be
killed with no warning or ability to defend yourself by RTI on a regular basis.

Cards that have that large an effect on the game (i.e. oust someone in a single
action while thay are at 12 pool), and will kill you unless you are holding a
specific card in your hand at the time it is played, are just wrong.

"Even if it's unblockable, which is often the case. You can deflect it with
either AUS or dom. 55% of the clans have this as in clan discaplines. Or if
your not in that group (like me who is an avid Gangrel fan, and even they have
5 vamps with Dominate) you can use the ever effective Archon Investigation. It
works every time."

Again, yes, you can Deflect it, however, if you are not playing a deck that
uses bleed bounce, and before RTI, decks without bleed bounce were perfectly
viable, you will be ousted every time. Thus you need to play bleed bounce to
be competetive. So everyone will be playing bleed bounce, and the last guy to
be bleed bounced to will be ousted, and as the original targer was the first
one to bounce, it is likely that he will be the last one bounced to, and thus
killed anyway.

Archon Investigation is not an acceptable answer either. Jyhad is a game of
strategies competeing against strategies, not hoser cards competeing against
hoser cards. With the RTI/AI war, the game boils down to little more than who
happens to be holding the particular "I Win" card at any particular time,
rather than who has built a better deck and knows how to use it more
effectively. Both cards are lame and should not have been included in the set,
although due to the inclusion of RTI, AI is now completely necessary (when
without RTI, it was not).

The original Jyhad set did not include Archon Investigation, and the game was
perfectly balanced. When they reprinted the set, someone decided that Archon
Investigation was a good idea (which is highly questionable), and it had a
profound effect on play balance (mostly that decks that went for few but big

austensibly the reason for AI in the first place, were completely unaffected).

control card like RTI, justifying it by saying "Well, they can always play with
AI...". Once RTI was in place and became a dominant card, there neded to be
more safeguards against it, because AI was not sufficient. Thus DI is born.
This cycle of hosers justifying hosers justifying hosers is just silly.

Well... just look at the Tomb, for one... It requires no clan, no discipline
and immediately pays back your investment with no risk. Even if you're using
Toreador, why use Art Museum over the Tomb? There's no reason to. The Tomb
can stay in play as long as you like, as long as you transfer pool off the
vamp with the Tomb, and it can give you more than 1 pool per influence
phase. So, in all respects, the Tomb is better than many other cards. This
breaks a fundamental tenet of Jyhad... that being that no card is basically
*better* than another. There shouldn't be any reason to use one card over
another in every possible situation. So, the Tomb is just plain wrong. Does
anyone have a valid argument that it is *not* better than Art Museum,
Ecoterrorists, Arcane Library, etc.?

Unfortunately, the issue is not quite so black-and-white with RtI. I
personally feel that common sense says that RtI is way overpowered. But
that's still an opinion. The main point is that the card basically gives you
a victory point at no risk. If the action is unsuccessful, you don't pay any
blood *or* lose a vampire. If the action *is* successful, you get a victory
point and 6 pool in return for a vampire. You can ignore the loss of your
vampire, as you've been able to use it for a few turns and have gotten some
benefit out of it. Either that, or you've minion tapped it so it only costs 4
pool (cost of RtI). So, basically, it's an action to gain a victory point and
2 pool. Sure, it can be blocked, but so can Computer Hacking. And Computer
Hacking is far from assured to give you a victory point. Neither has any
risk. Even Dominate and Presence, two bleeding disciplines don't have nearly
as much power as RtI, which is disciplineless. RtI has no requirement except
that the vampire have 4 blood. Lots of vampires have 4 blood. This is not a
large requirement. So it becomes: Played by a vampire with at least 4 blood,
if your prey does not block, he is ousted and this vampire is burned. Let me
reiterate that there is *no risk.* If you don't succeeed, your vampire stays
alive and doesn't even lose 4 blood. I feel that a card with this much power
must have some sort of risk. I would even be happy with a fix that said "this
vampire is burned even if the action is unsuccessful." This wouldn't stop
Gangrel's from being able to unblockably bleed like super-Malks, but it would
at least keep this from being put indiscriminately into every deck.

Other cards I think are less in need of fixing. It makes sense for Thoughts
Betrayed to only be usable against allies and younger vampires, or for it to
cost 3 blood instead of 2. As it is, it's too strong, but I could live
without fixing it. Same for Mind Rape. Direct Intervention is just a
disgusting card that's not in the spirit of the game and should be banned.
(Of course, I feel the same way about Sudden Reversal...). And... as I said
before, fixing Zip Gun is just silly.

-Chris

>Dreams is not outright better than Short Term.

Well, no, it's not outright better. It's also unique and inferior in
that sense. The same is true of Tomb not being outright better than
Art Museum et al, as described in Legbiter's post right near here.

Here's how I'd look at it tho...
advantages of dreams:
- takes 1 master phase for full benefit instead of 4
- get full benefits one turn faster because you don't have to wait for
a master phase to start using it
- usually gets you 3 free transfers in the process
- can be used for extra cards in your hand if you really need it

advantages of STI:
- not unique
- can be used if you have neither the edge nor an uncontrolled vamp

The uniqueness typically isn't a problem since you wait for the one
that's out to go away before you play yours.

And I've never run into a case where I couldn't use it at the end of a
game. Worst case you can transfer a new vamp to uncontrolled and
still gain one pool out of the deal 2 turns later. Plus you have a
new uncontrolled vamp.

It's enough better that I'd always use it over STI, which is enough
better for it to bother me.

Magic and Jyhad are the same basic type of game and have the same
basic premise. Within that structure they're pretty different, but
that structure does make them pretty similar as compared to other
games in general...

Both are card games where you build a deck from a set of cards of
differing rarities, etc., etc., etc. Deck design, skill within the
game, and luck are all important factors in both.

In both games you play some powerful controlling being who has some
health meter (life or pool) and when you run out of health you're out
of the game. Your goal is to make everyone else run out of health
before you do (in a certain order for Jyhad).

You have minions that you summon to do your dirty work for you. You
send them to go attack the other players and reduce their health. The
other players use their minions to try to stop that. If they run into
each other, they fight about it.

Everyone takes turns and in a turn you replenish all your resources
(untap), take whatever actions you're going to, etc.

On other people's turns you can block or play cards from a limited
subset of the card set.

You can do things to make your minions cooler, or you can do some
direct effects (masters).

The games put different emphases on different parts and implement it
all rather differently, but the basic idea is about the same.
Jyhad has a lot more depth to it, I think, but (at the risk of
blaspheming) Magic isn't that bad a game either. If the cards were at
the same prices as Jyhad cards, I might still play it some. As it is,
I sold off my deck and a few other cards for several hundred dollars a
few years ago and ended up making some money on the whole deal.

Jyhad is a good game if you want interesting multiplayer dynamics and
a thoughtful game. It requires a lot more planning and diplomacy and
less brute force of powerful cards and combos. That's somewhat less
true of combat decks, which is why I don't really like them.

Magic is fun if you don't have anything to do for half an hour, and I
actually think it involves more intricate work in doing a good job
playing the cards you have. And all the editions have the same backs
:)

Jyhad is strategic and Magic is tactical, if you will.
Of course, Magic is tactical only if you've spent about as much on
your deck as your opponent.
